concepts.definition: A DNA sequence that contributes to a functional RNA or protein product.
One alternative DNA form of a gene at a particular locus.
Physical position of a gene or DNA marker on a chromosome.
Long DNA molecule with associated proteins that carries many genes.
A maternal and paternal chromosome pair bearing corresponding gene loci, potentially with different alleles.
The two DNA copies produced by chromosome replication, joined until they separate.
Chromosomal region where sister chromatid cohesion and kinetochore assembly support segregation.
Having two chromosome sets, usually one inherited from each parent.
Having one chromosome set, as in ordinary gametes.
Haploid reproductive cell that can combine with another during fertilization.
Two successive nuclear divisions following one DNA replication, usually yielding haploid products.
Reductional division that separates homologous chromosomes into different daughter cells.
Division that separates sister chromatids without a second preceding DNA replication.
Meiotic stage when homologues pair and recombination occurs.
Paired homologous chromosomes composed of four chromatids.
DNA exchange between nonsister chromatids of paired homologues during meiosis I.
Stage when homologous chromosome pairs align at the cell equator.
Stage when homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles.
Stage when sister chromatids separate during meiosis II.
Reproduction from one parental source, often yielding offspring genetically similar to that parent.
Reproduction involving gametes and the combination of genetic contributions.
Nuclear division that normally preserves chromosome-set number and distributes sister chromatids.
Individual or cell derived from a common ancestor and usually genetically very similar.
Union of gametes that forms a zygote and restores the diploid chromosome number in typical animal life cycles.
Cell produced from the union of gametes.
Independent distribution of unlinked chromosome pairs or genes into gametes.
Chance combination of genetically different gametes from two parents.
Heritable change in DNA sequence and ultimate source of new alleles.
Scientist whose controlled pea crosses established particulate principles of inheritance.
Hereditary units remain distinct across generations rather than permanently blending.
Heritable feature, such as flower color, that may occur in alternative forms.
Particular variant of a heritable character, such as purple flowers.
Allelic constitution or genetic makeup of an organism at specified loci.
Observable characteristics arising from genotype, development and environment.
Having two identical alleles at the specified diploid locus.
Having two different alleles at the specified diploid locus.
Allele whose associated phenotype is expressed in a heterozygote under complete dominance.
Alleles of a diploid gene separate during gamete formation so typical gametes receive one.
Grid enumerating possible combinations of parental gamete alleles.
Cross tracking the inheritance of one gene or character.
Cross of a dominant-phenotype unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive tester.
Numerical measure of the likelihood of an outcome, from zero to one.
Multiply probabilities for two independent outcomes both occurring.
Add probabilities for mutually exclusive alternative outcomes.
Expected proportion of offspring genotypes from a particular cross.
Expected proportion of offspring displaying each phenotype.
Expected allele or offspring proportions produced by a given cross under its assumptions.
Cross tracing offspring outcomes for two genes or traits.
Different genes segregate independently when their allele transmissions are unlinked.
Genes located on the same chromosome and often inherited together.
Both alleles contribute distinguishable expressions in the heterozygote.
More than two allele forms of one locus exist in a population.
Human blood-type system with Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i alleles; Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant.
A single gene influences multiple phenotypic characteristics.
One phenotype influenced by variants at multiple genes.
Variation in phenotype depending on both inherited variants and environmental conditions.
Condition typically requiring two relevant pathogenic alleles at a diploid locus for expression.
Condition that can be expressed with one pathogenic allele at a diploid locus.
Mating between genetically related individuals, increasing homozygosity and matching allele inheritance.
Presence of two matching alleles at a particular diploid locus.
Classic hybrid derived from radish and cabbage whose fertility can be restored after chromosome doubling.
Offspring arising from parents of genetically distinct lines or taxa.
Hybrid unable to produce viable functional gametes under ordinary conditions.
Increase in complete chromosome sets, sometimes restoring homologous partners for meiotic pairing.
Presence of multiplied chromosome sets derived from distinct species or evolutionary lineages.
Theory that genes occupy particular loci on chromosomes whose behavior explains Mendelian inheritance.
Geneticist who used fruit-fly studies to link hereditary traits to chromosomes.
Fruit-fly model organism with a short generation time, many offspring and four chromosome pairs.
Common or reference phenotype in a studied population.
Observable variant that differs from the standard wild-type form.
Morgan's classic mutant fruit-fly eye-color trait used to reveal X-linked inheritance.
Common fruit-fly eye-color trait contrasted with the white-eye mutation in Morgan's crosses.
Chromosomes involved in sex determination; X and Y in typical human XX/XY development.
Defined place along a chromosome where a particular gene is located.
Gene located on a sex chromosome, producing inheritance patterns affected by sex-chromosome transmission.
Gene carried on the X chromosome.
Gene carried on the Y chromosome and normally passed along Y-bearing lineages.
Having one gene copy at a locus normally represented by two in another chromosome complement.
Transmission of genetic material chiefly through the mother in the relevant biological system.
Genetic material outside the nucleus, including mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes.
Small DNA genome within mitochondria, commonly transmitted through the egg in humans.
DNA within plastids that supports some organelle functions and can show lineage-specific inheritance.
Presence of cell populations arising from more than one zygote or fertilization lineage in one individual.
Deoxyribonucleic acid; the principal information-storing genetic polymer in cellular organisms.
Virus that infects bacteria, used in classic experiments on genetic information.
1952 phage-labeling study showing DNA, rather than most phage protein, enters bacteria and directs infection.
Isotope used to label phage DNA in Hershey–Chase experiments because DNA contains phosphorus.
Isotope used to label phage protein because certain amino acids contain sulfur.
Agitation detaching phage protein coats from the surfaces of infected bacterial cells.
Separation by spinning that placed bacterial cells in a pellet and detached phage coats in the supernatant.
Dense material collected at the bottom of a centrifuge tube, containing bacterial cells in the experiment.
Liquid above the pellet, containing many detached phage coats in the experiment.
Building block made of nitrogenous base, pentose sugar and phosphate group.
Double-ring nitrogenous base class, including adenine and guanine.
Single-ring nitrogenous base class, including cytosine, thymine and uracil.
Preferential A–T and G–C pairing in DNA, and A–U when appropriate in RNA.
Covalently linked alternating sugar and phosphate units forming a nucleic acid strand.
Two antiparallel DNA strands paired inside a helical structure with an approximately 2-nm diameter.
Ribonucleic acid, commonly single-stranded and built with ribose and uracil instead of thymine.
Template-directed copying of DNA so daughter molecules preserve sequence information.
Mechanism in which each daughter DNA duplex contains one preexisting and one newly synthesized strand.
Accuracy of copying DNA, supported by nucleotide selectivity, proofreading and repair.
Processes that use genetic information to produce RNA and, for protein-coding genes, proteins.
Synthesis of RNA using a DNA template.
RNA carrying an encoded sequence read by ribosomes during translation.
Ribosome-directed synthesis of a polypeptide using mRNA codons.
Ribonucleoprotein machine that reads mRNA and assembles a polypeptide.
Three-nucleotide mRNA sequence specifying an amino acid or a stop signal.
Molecular building block joined into polypeptide chains during translation.
Chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds that may fold into a functional protein.
Rules mapping mRNA codons to amino acids or translation-stop instructions.
Most living organisms use essentially the same codon assignments with limited exceptions.
Inheritance of traits with changes accumulating across generations, producing branching lineages.
Change in inherited characteristics of populations across generations.
Branching hypothesis of evolutionary relationships among lineages.
Scientific naming convention using a genus and species epithet.
Naturalist who formalized binomial nomenclature in Systema Naturae.
Early evolutionist known for a historical account involving inheritance of acquired characteristics.
Naturalist who developed and publicized evolution by natural selection, including in 1859.
Naturalist who independently developed natural selection and communicated his ideas with Darwin.
Prominent 19th-century defender of evolutionary theory known as Darwin's Bulldog.
Darwin's 1859 book presenting evidence and argument for evolution by natural selection.
Differential survival and reproduction of inherited variants under particular environments.
DNA sequence change that creates new inherited allele variants.
Random change in allele frequencies due to chance sampling across generations.
Geographic division of a population or range by a new barrier.
Selection arising from variation in mating success, including mate choice and competition.
Relative genetic contribution of an individual or genotype to future generations in a given environment.
Proportion of gene copies at a locus represented by a specified allele in a population.
Genetically transmissible differences among individuals that may affect traits and fitness.
Environmental or reproductive factor producing differences in survival or reproductive success among inherited variants.
Barriers limiting successful gene exchange among lineages.
Reproductive barrier acting before fertilization or zygote formation.
Barrier acting after fertilization, reducing hybrid viability or fertility.
Species criterion emphasizing reproductive compatibility within groups and isolation from other groups.
Evolutionary emergence of distinct species lineages.
Reduced ability of a hybrid to produce functional gametes or offspring.
Geologically brief episode of widespread species losses across many lineages.
Rapid diversification of a lineage into multiple forms occupying distinct ecological opportunities.
Evolutionary patterns and processes at or above species level, including lineage splitting and extinction.
